claim: Tobacco smoking and alcohol consumption are leading causes of the global burden of disease and are major contributors to premature mortality.
source: Tobacco smoking and alcohol consumption are leading causes of the global burden of disease and are major contributors to premature mortality (GBD 2016 Alcohol Collaborators, 2018; GBD 2016 Alcohol Collaborators, 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to GBD 2016 Alcohol Collaborators studies from 2018 and 2020.

claim: Gastrointestinal diseases account for considerable health care use and expenditures.
source: Gastrointestinal diseases account for considerable health care use and expenditures, and a holistic approach to lifestyle interventions may result in more health gains and less economic burdens (Peery et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Peery et al., 2022.

claim: Tobacco smoking has been identified as a risk factor for gastroesophageal reflux disease.
source: Population-based studies have identified tobacco smoking as a risk factor for several gastrointestinal diseases, including gastroesophageal reflux disease (Eusebi et al., 2018), esophageal cancer (Fund WCR and Research AIfC, 2007), Crohn's disease (Piovani et al., 2019), liver cancer (McGee et al., 2019), and pancreatitis (Yadav and Whitcomb, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Eusebi et al., 2018.

claim: Tobacco smoking has been identified as a risk factor for esophageal cancer.

evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Fund WCR and Research AIfC, 2007.

evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Yadav and Whitcomb, 2010.

claim: Heavy alcohol consumption has been associated with increased risk of gastritis.
source: Like smoking, heavy alcohol consumption has been associated with increased risk of several gastrointestinal outcomes, including gastritis (Bujanda, 2000), gastric cancer (Laszkowska et al., 2021), colorectal cancer (McNabb et al., 2020), cirrhosis (Simpson et al., 2019), liver cancer (McGee et al., 2019), and pancreatitis (Yadav and Whitcomb, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bujanda, 2000.

claim: Heavy alcohol consumption has been associated with increased risk of gastric cancer.

claim: Smoking and alcohol consumption are phenotypically and genetically correlated.
source: In addition, as smoking and alcohol consumption are phenotypically and genetically correlated (Roberts et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2019), the independent impacts of smoking and alcohol consumption on gastrointestinal diseases are unclear.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Roberts et al., 2020 and Liu et al., 2019.

claim: Mendelian randomization is an epidemiological approach that utilizes genetic variants as an instrument to strengthen the causal inference in an exposure-outcome association.
source: Mendelian randomization (MR) is an epidemiological approach that utilizes genetic variants as an instrument to strengthen the causal inference in an exposure-outcome association (Davey Smith and Hemani, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Davey Smith and Hemani, 2014.

claim: MR is by nature not prone to confounding since genetic variants are randomly assorted at conception and thus unrelated to environmental and self-adopted factors that usually act as confounders.
source: MR is by nature not prone to confounding since genetic variants are randomly assorted at conception and thus unrelated to environmental and self-adopted factors that usually act as confounders.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about Mendelian randomization methodology and genetic inheritance.

claim: MR can minimize reverse causality since fixed alleles are unaffected by the onset and progression of disease.
source: Additionally, this method can minimize reverse causality since fixed alleles are unaffected by the onset and progression of disease.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about Mendelian randomization methodology and genetic inheritance.

claim: A total of 378 SNPs were associated with smoking initiation at the genome-wide significance level in the GSCAN study.
source: A total of 378 and 99 single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) associated with smoking initiation (a binary phenotype indicating whether an individual had ever being a regular smoker, 1,232,091 individuals of European descent) and alcohol consumption (log-transformed drinks per week, 941,280 individuals of European descent) at the genome-wide significance threshold (p<5 × 10–8) were identified by the GWAS and Sequencing Consortium of Alcohol and Nicotine use (GSCAN) study (Liu et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Liu et al., 2019 and describes data from the GSCAN study.

claim: A total of 99 SNPs were associated with alcohol consumption at the genome-wide significance level in the GSCAN study.
source: A total of 378 and 99 single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) associated with smoking initiation (a binary phenotype indicating whether an individual had ever being a regular smoker, 1,232,091 individuals of European descent) and alcohol consumption (log-transformed drinks per week, 941,280 individuals of European descent) at the genome-wide significance threshold (p<5 × 10–8) were identified by the GWAS and Sequencing Consortium of Alcohol and Nicotine use (GSCAN) study (Liu et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Liu et al., 2019 and describes data from the GSCAN study.

claim: The SNPs for smoking initiation explained approximately 2.3% of the variation in smoking initiation.
source: These SNPs explained approximately 2.3 and 0.3% of the variation in smoking initiation and alcohol consumption, respectively (Liu et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Liu et al., 2019.

claim: The SNPs for alcohol consumption explained approximately 0.3% of the variation in alcohol consumption.
source: These SNPs explained approximately 2.3 and 0.3% of the variation in smoking initiation and alcohol consumption, respectively (Liu et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Liu et al., 2019.

claim: After removing SNPs in linkage disequilibrium, 314 independent SNPs remained as instrumental variables for smoking initiation.
source: SNPs in linkage disequilibrium (defined as r2 >0.01 or clump distance <10,000 kb) and with the weaker associations with the exposure were removed, leaving 314 independent SNPs as instrumental variables for smoking initiation and 84 for alcohol consumption.
evidence: The claim describes the data processing methods used in the study.

claim: After removing SNPs in linkage disequilibrium, 84 independent SNPs remained as instrumental variables for alcohol consumption.
source: SNPs in linkage disequilibrium (defined as r2 >0.01 or clump distance <10,000 kb) and with the weaker associations with the exposure were removed, leaving 314 independent SNPs as instrumental variables for smoking initiation and 84 for alcohol consumption.
evidence: The claim describes the data processing methods used in the study.

claim: Smoking initiation and alcohol consumption shared two index genetic variants: rs1713676 and rs11692435.
source: Smoking initiation and alcohol consumption shared two index genetic variants, which were rs1713676 and rs11692435.
evidence: The claim describes the genetic variants identified in the study.

claim: There was around 30% sample overlap between the GSCAN study with full data and the UK Biobank study.
source: Considering partial sample overlap (around 30%) between the GSCAN study with full data and the UK Biobank study (Liu et al., 2019), we performed sensitivity analyses for smoking initiation and alcohol consumption using summary statistics data from the analysis excluding the UK Biobank and 23andMe.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Liu et al., 2019.

claim: 126 SNPs were associated with a lifetime smoking index that considered smoking duration, heaviness, and cessation.
source: For a supplementary analysis of smoking behavior, we used 126 SNPs associated with a lifetime smoking index that considered smoking duration, heaviness, and cessation (Wootton et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Wootton et al., 2020.

claim: The set of genetic instruments for lifetime smoking captured around 0.36% of the variance in lifetime smoking.
source: The set of genetic instruments captured around 0.36% of the variance in lifetime smoking (Wootton et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Wootton et al., 2020.

claim: The UK Biobank study is a large multicenter cohort study of 500,000 participants recruited in the United Kingdom between 2006 and 2010.
source: The UK Biobank study is a large multicenter cohort study of 500,000 participants recruited in the United Kingdom between 2006 and 2010 (Sudlow et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Sudlow et al., 2015.

claim: The F-statistic for each genetic variant was above 10, suggesting a good strength of used genetic instruments.
source: The F-statistic for each genetic variant was above 10, suggesting a good strength of used genetic instruments (Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: The claim is based on statistical analysis of the genetic instruments used in the study.

claim: For smoking initiation, there was 80% power to detect the smallest odds ratio ranging from 1.08 to 1.40 for included outcomes.
source: For smoking initiation, there was 80% power to detect the smallest odds ratio (OR) ranging from 1.08 to 1.40 for included outcomes.
evidence: The claim is based on power analysis calculations performed for the study.

claim: Genetic predisposition to smoking initiation was associated with 20 of the 24 studied gastrointestinal diseases.
source: Genetic predisposition to smoking initiation was associated with 20 of the 24 studied gastrointestinal diseases, and all these associations remained after multiple comparison correction (Table 1 and Supplementary file 1E).
evidence: The claim is based on the Mendelian randomization analysis results presented in the study.
